What is a public IP address?

Every device on the internet is reachable through an IP address. The address shown above is your public IP: the one websites and servers see when you connect. Inside your home or office your devices usually have private addresses such as 192.168.1.20 or 10.0.0.5; your router translates them to a single public address using NAT. That is why every device on the same network shows the same public IP.

IPv4 versus IPv6

IPv4 addresses are four numbers separated by dots (203.0.113.9) and there are only about 4.3 billion of them. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits written in hexadecimal (2001:db8::1), which gives a practically unlimited supply. Many networks are dual-stack and have both. If the IPv6 box above says "Not detected", your provider or network probably does not offer IPv6 yet.

How accurate is the location?

IP geolocation is approximate. It is built from registry data, routing information and measurement, and usually identifies the country and often the city of your provider's network, not your street address. Mobile networks, VPNs, corporate proxies and carrier-grade NAT frequently place users in a different city or even a different country.

What do ISP and ASN mean?

Your ISP is the company that provides your connection. The ASN (Autonomous System Number) identifies the network that announces your IP range on the internet through BGP. Click the ASN above to see its prefixes, neighbours and RPKI status in our BGP and ASN lookup.

Frequently asked questions

Why is my IP address different from the one in my network settings?

Your device settings show a private address assigned by your router. The address on this page is the public address your router or your ISP presents to the internet.

Does my IP address change?

Most residential connections use dynamic addresses that can change when your router restarts or your lease expires. Business connections often have static addresses. Mobile networks change addresses frequently.

Why does my IP show a different city or country?

Geolocation databases map address ranges to where the provider registered or routes them. A VPN, a mobile carrier, a corporate proxy or an out-of-date database entry can all produce a location that differs from where you are.

Can I hide my IP address?

You can mask it by using a VPN, a proxy or a service such as Tor. Websites then see the address of that service instead of your own. Your ISP still sees that you are connected to it.

What data does this page send?

Your browser requests your address from a public IP detection service and, for the location details, from an IP geolocation service. See the privacy policy for details.
